title: The city of nine gates
hookLine: a stranger in a Varanasi lane asks Shankara which self should move aside, and the Gita explains the answer
carry: the same self sits in every body
last: RENOUNCE OR ACT — BOTH REACH THE GOAL.

cards: Varanasi, on the river Ganga, more than a thousand years ago. The teacher Shankara is walking by the river with his students.
In a narrow lane, a man comes the other way with four dogs: a man the society of that day treated as untouchable. Shankara tells him: move aside. The man doesn't move.
He asks a question instead. Which should move away from which? This body, made of food, from that body, made of food?
Or the self in me from the self in you, when it's the same self? Shankara stops. And he bows.

teach.b: That's a story told about Shankara; in many tellings the stranger was Shiva himself. Shankara answered in verse: whoever truly sees this, born outcaste or born a priest, is my teacher.
The idea is the Gita's, chapter five. Verse thirteen: the one who lives in the body sits at ease in the city of nine gates.

teach.h: NINE GATES: EYES, EARS, NOSTRILS, MOUTH…
teach.b: The nine gates are the body's openings: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, the mouth, and the two openings for waste. And who lives in the city?
An old word-play hears purusha, the person, as the one who dwells in the pura, the city.

Hindus call that dweller the atman: the self, the real you. Many teachers, Shankara among them, say it is one with Brahman, God in everything. The doing, verse fourteen says, is nature doing what nature does.
Then verse eighteen, the verse the man in the lane was living: the wise look with the same eye at a learned priest, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a person society shuns.

teach.h: THE SAME EYE ON EVERY BEING.
teach.b: Because the same one is seated in every city. It's why many Hindus greet with folded hands, namaste, I bow to you, and many explain it as a bow to the divine in you.
Today it meets the people you look past: the person cleaning the office, the kid nobody sits with.

teach.h: THE SAME SELF IN EVERY BODY.

how: Hindus greet with folded hands and namaste (literally 'I bow to you'), which many explain as a bow to the self or the divine in the other; in meditation, some draw attention inward from the senses, the 'gates' of Gita 5.13.

o: the one who dwells in the body
the body with its nine gates
a king who rules a walled city

games.q: what's inside the city — tap the pairs.
p: see every being with the same eye

s: namaste literally means 'the divine in me bows to the divine in you'
literally it's 'i bow to you'. the bow to the divine in the other is how many Hindus explain it.
verse 18 says the wise see a cow, a dog and a priest with the same eye
the same one is seated in every city, so the wise look at every being alike.
verse 14 says the Lord makes us feel we're the doers
verse 14 says the reverse: the Lord doesn't create the sense of doing; nature does what nature does.

games.q: a man with four dogs won't move aside for a great teacher. by verse 18, how do the wise see him?
o: below the teacher, so he should move.
with the same eye: the same self is in both.
above the teacher, because he's humble.
games.why: with the same eye: sama-darshinah. the same atman is seated in every body, so Shankara bowed.

practice: Visit the gates one at a time: your eyes, noticing light; your ears, the nearest sound, then the farthest; your nostrils, the cool air coming in. You don't have to close any gate. Notice that something in the middle is noticing.
Then bring to mind one person you passed today without really seeing, and silently, hands folded if you like, say namaste to the one seated in them.

wordCard.voice: Purusha. The person, the one who dwells in the city. Hindus call that dweller the atman, the self: seated at ease behind the nine gates, and the same in every body.

orig.note: Sanskrit: nava-dvare pure, 'in the city of nine gates'. nava, nine; dvara, door; pura, city.

carryVoice: Carry this: the same self sits in every body. The same eye for the priest, the dog, and the man in the lane. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 5.13 (the city of nine gates)
Shvetashvatara Upanishad 3.18; Katha Upanishad 2.2.1 (the body as a city with gates); Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.5.18 (purusha as the one dwelling in every city)
The chandala episode at Varanasi, traditionally framing the Manisha Panchakam (attributed to Shankara); also told in Madhava-Vidyaranya's Shankara-digvijaya
